messages.author: cefd17aea0d7c422
messages.subject: pharmacokinetic modeling with R2Jags or rstan
parts:
Dear All,
 
I’m not quite familiar with Bayesian statistics (and stan in particular), but think that it might provide a solution for my pharmacokinetic problem. What I'm trying to do is individual parameter estimation of a subject with 2 measurements and use an established PopPK model. The Bayesian approach seems suitable to use prior information of the published parameters to obtain individual posterior estimates, am I right? Unfortunately, the model is a bit complicated, i.e. a three-compartment model of a infusion.
 
I found a blog by Wingfeet applying R2Jags, adapted it, but received an error message:
 
                Error in jags.model(model.file, data = data, inits = init.values, n.chains = n.chains,  :
                Error in node V2
                Invalid parent values
 
Can you image what is wrong? And is this example transferable to be approached by stan in R?
 
Many thanks and best wishes
 
Andreas
 
 
 
R code for the R2jags approach (currently not working!) that sets the framework for potential adaptions to stan:
 
library(R2jags)
individual <- data.frame(
  time=c(0,216,240),
  conc=c(0,0.00473, 0.00409))
datain <- as.list(individual)
datain$n <- nrow(ch10sp4)
#datain$Rinf <- 1*100
 
model1 <- function() {
 
  # concentration formula
    tau <- 1/pow(sigma,2)
    sigma ~ dunif(0,100)
    # infusion time = 0
    for (i in 1:n) {
      #pred[i] <- ifelse(time[i] <= 1,
      #                  dose*((A/alpha * (1 - exp(-alpha*time[i]))) + (B/beta * (1 - exp(-beta*time[i]))) + (C/gamma * (1 - exp(-gamma*time[i])))),
      #                  dose*((A/alpha * (1 - exp(-alpha*1)) * exp(-alpha*(time[i]-1))) +
      #                    (B/beta * (1 - exp(-beta*1)) * exp(-beta*(time[i]-1))) +
      #                    (C/gamma * (1 - exp(-gamma*1)) * exp(-gamma*(time[i]-1)))))
      pred[i] <- dose*((A/alpha * (1 - exp(-alpha*1)) * exp(-alpha*(time[i]-1))) +
                                (B/beta * (1 - exp(-beta*1)) * exp(-beta*(time[i]-1))) +
                                (C/gamma * (1 - exp(-gamma*1)) * exp(-gamma*(time[i]-1))))
      conc[i] ~ dnorm(pred[i],tau)
    }
 
  # micro constants
    V <- V1
    k <- CL/V1
    k12 <- Q2/V1
    k21 <- Q2/V2
    k13 <- Q3/V1
    k31 <- Q3/V3
 
  # macro constants
    a0 <- k*k21*k31
    a1 <- k*k31 + k21*k31 + k21*k13 + k*k21 + k31*k12
    a2 <- k + k12 + k13 + k21 + k31
    p <- a1 - (a2^2)/3
    q <- ((2* a2^3)/27 ) - (a1*(a2/3)) + a0
    r1 <- sqrt(-((p^3)/27))
    r2 <- 2 * (r1^(1/3))
    phi <- (acos(-(q)/(2*r1))) / 3
    alpha <- -( (cos(phi) * r2) - a2/3 )
    beta <- -( (cos(phi + (2*3.141593/3) ) * r2) - a2/3 )
    gamma <- -( (cos(phi + (4*3.141593/3) ) * r2) - a2/3 )
    A <- 1/V * ((k21-alpha)/(alpha-beta)) * ((k31-alpha)/(alpha-gamma))
    B <- 1/V * ((k21-beta)/(beta-alpha)) * ((k31-beta)/(beta-gamma))
    C <- 1/V * ((k21-gamma)/(gamma-beta)) * ((k31-gamma)/(gamma-alpha))
 
  # prior information from published model
    CL~dlnorm(log(44.1),log(44.1*0.06))
    V1~dlnorm(log(8.9),log(8.9*0.09))
    Q2~dlnorm(log(6.1),log(6.1*0.07))
    V2~dlnorm(log(7.3),log(7.3*0.09))
    Q3~dlnorm(log(14.4),log(14.4*0.12))
    V3~dlnorm(log(388),log(388*0.11))
 
}
 
 
parameters <- c('CL','V1','Q2','V2','Q3','V3')
inits <- function()
  list(CL=rlnorm(1,log(44),.1),V1=rlnorm(1,log(9),.1),
       Q2=rlnorm(1,log(6),.1), V2=rlnorm(1,log(7),.1),
       Q3=rlnorm(1,log(14),.1), V3=rlnorm(1,log(388),.1),
       sigma=rlnorm(1,1,.1))
jagsfit <- jags(datain, model=model1,
                inits=inits,
                parameters=parameters,progress.bar="gui",
                n.chains=4,n.iter=14000,n.burnin=5000,n.thin=2)

Yes, you can translate that almost line for line. Stan
parameterizes the normal (and lognormal) with scale (std dev),
whereas JAGS/BUGS use precision (inverse variance).

- Bob

messages.author: cefd17aea0d7c422
messages.subject: Re: pharmacokinetic modeling with R2Jags or rstan
parts:
Dear Álvaro and Bob,

thanks for these notes. Indeed, the code runs with a positive tau. This brings me back to a more basic issue, how to use "informative" priors based on a published PopPK model. The model is reported as follows:

                                                                Typical value (CV%)     IIV (CV%)
CL Total plasma clearance (l h-1)                 44.1 (6%)                   29.4% (15%)
V1 Volume central compartment  (l)               8.9 (9%)                   37.8% (14%)
Q2 Intercompartmental CL (C1-C2) (l h-1)       6.1 (7%)        
V2 Volume peripheral compartment (l)           7.3 (9%)        
Q3 Intercompartmental Cl (C2-C3) (l h-1)      14.4 (12%)                  20.3% (20%)
V3 Volume peripheral compartment (l)        388 (11%)        
_______________________________________________________________________
CV, covariance; IIV, inter individual variability.

In specifying the PK model (either R2Jags or stan), how to I appropriately incorporate this prior information? Do I have to introduce omegas for the inter-individual variability, as well. And is it correct, to write for example CL~dlnorm(log(44.1),log(44.1)*0.06) and omega_CL~dlnorm(log(0.294),log(0.294)*0.15)?

Best wishes

Andreas

In the book of A. Gelman: Bayesian Data Analysis, there is a example (19.2 Example: population toxicokinetics) where there is a description of how to set up the prior information of this kind of problems.

Álvaro.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] pharmacokinetic modeling with R2Jags or rstan
parts:
I don't know what IIV or CV are, but I can say that the section
of BDA comes from the Gelman and Bois JASA paper on
the same topic.

In general, you want the prior to put most of the mass where you
think the answer is going to be --- that is, on reasonable values.
This is in contrast to very wide (sometimes misleadingly called
"uninformative") priors (miseading because they can have a big
effect).

We usually don't trust former experiments exact numbers,
so we usually relax them a bit. Or we create a meta-analysis
model to include the data from multiple experiments.

- Bob
